explanation: Option A is correct because the query must join employee to itself using aliases, one alias for the employee row and one for the manager row. The condition e.manager_id = m.emp_id matches each employee to the manager row, and LEFT JOIN keeps employees whose manager_id is NULL. Option B uses an undefined table and the wrong relationship direction. Option C returns the manager id rather than the manager's name. Option D joins each employee row to itself instead of to that employee's manager.

options.text: SELECT e.emp_name, m.emp_name AS manager_name FROM employee e LEFT JOIN employee m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;
SELECT e.emp_name, m.emp_name AS manager_name FROM employee e JOIN manager m ON e.emp_id = m.manager_id;
SELECT emp_name, manager_id FROM employee WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL;

explanation: A row that can point to another row in the same table through a foreign key is a recursive relationship. Because each product can reference at most one predecessor, the mapping is recursive one-to-many: many products may share the same predecessor, while each product points to at most one predecessor.

It is a one-to-one relationship because each product has at most one predecessor
